author: hlntnr
text: We actually already have something almost as good as perfect instantaneous translation - human interpreters! They're just expensive. But I bet if you ask any polyglot whether they'd swap that skill for a free multilingual interpreter, they'd turn you down. I certainly would. 5/5

author: hlntnr
text: Lossy: languages don't map perfectly onto each other. Different languages make it easier to express some concepts than others, or combine connotation & denotation in different ways. This makes it impossible to fully grasp what someone is saying if you only hear a translation. 4/5

author: hlntnr
text: Few-second delays might not sound like a big deal, but they make a huge difference to how a conversation feels. Turn-taking, clarification, nonverbal cues are all much more stilted. This matters less for pure exchange-of-facts conversations, but most communication isn't that. 3/5

author: hlntnr
text: Laggy: languages have different grammatical structures, so even with instant transcription & translation, the AI will often need to wait for the end of a phrase or sentence to know what has been said. This means the conversation is riddled with few-second delays. 2/5

author: hlntnr
text:
No. Sorry to pick on you @SpencrGreenberg, but I hear this often and it's just wrong. 

Machine translation will make it easier to read text in other languages, but translation *in conversation* will always be noticeably laggy & lossy compared to conversing in one language. 1/5

quoted.text:
• Learning a foreign language. If machine translation becomes good enough, we’ll be able to converse accurately (in almost real time) in other languages. 

It might be a lot more fun to know the language, and necessary for some purposes, but it won’t be needed for understanding
